questions.question: Define adaptation and explain, using the gemsbok, one structural, one functional and one behavioural adaptation, stating the habitat problem each solves.
questions.expected_answer: An adaptation is an inherited feature that increases an organism's chance of surviving and reproducing in its habitat. Gemsbok, Kalahari heat and drought: structural — pale coat reflects sunlight, keeping the body cooler; functional — allows body temperature to rise above 45 °C by day and cools blood to the brain via nasal blood vessels, saving water that sweating would lose; behavioural — feeds at night and early morning when plants hold most moisture, and digs up water-storing roots and tsamma melons.

questions.question: Define extinction and give two natural and three human causes. Explain why adaptations do not protect a species from extinction when its environment changes rapidly.
questions.expected_answer: Extinction: a species has no living individuals left anywhere; it is permanent. Natural causes: long-term climate change, asteroid impact (dinosaurs, 66 million years ago), volcanic eruptions, disease, competition from new species. Human causes: habitat destruction, hunting/overharvesting, alien invasive species, pollution, human-driven climate change. Adaptations are inherited features that fit the habitat as it was and change only over many generations; if the habitat disappears or conditions shift within decades, the adaptations no longer match and the species cannot adjust in time.

questions.question: Name two South African species that are extinct and three that are threatened, with the human cause in each case.
questions.expected_answer: Extinct: quagga (hunted for meat and hides and to clear grazing for sheep; last died 1883) and bluebuck (hunting and conversion of its grassland to farms; around 1800). Also Cape lion, Cape warthog. Threatened: riverine rabbit (riverside Karoo vegetation ploughed and grazed); African penguin (overfishing of sardines and anchovies, oil spills, guano and egg collecting); black rhino (poaching for horn); Knysna seahorse (estuary pollution and development); Pickersgill's reed frog (wetland drainage); Clanwilliam cedar (timber cutting, too-frequent fire).
